title: Few-Shot Design Optimization by Exploiting Auxiliary Information
claim: Experiments yield rich auxiliary feedback beyond the reward, and a context-conditioned predictor can use it in a closed optimization loop.
layout: 2 panels split by dotted line; left examples, right loop flowchart
description: The figure has two panels separated by a vertical dotted line. Panel (a), on the left, shows two example design problems. The first is a robotic gripper holding a bottle. It has labeled renderings for the design x, the grasp stability f(x), and tactile feedback h(x) shown as hand icons. The second is hyperparameter tuning. It shows a small neural network diagram for x, a learning-curve plot with a star marking best validation accuracy for f(x), and validation and training accuracy curves for h(x). Panel (b), on the right, is a flowchart of blue and orange boxes with arrows. A model P_theta(.|C_t, x) takes observations C_t and a candidate x and predicts f-hat(x). That prediction feeds a box that picks x_{t+1}. A box then evaluates and observes f and h, and a feedback arrow adds the new observation to the context. Colors are blue boxes with one orange model box.
caption: Few-shot design optimization with our method. Part (a) shows examples of two design optimization problems in our setting, where for each problem, the design x is indicated, the reward f(x) evaluating design quality is shown, and the auxiliary information h(x) obtained when evaluating a design is indicated. The first problem involves designing a robotic gripper that grasps an object as stably as possible, using tactile feedback of the object during each grasp attempt. In the second problem, evaluating a hyperparameter setting returns per-epoch learning curves as h(x), which can provide useful information beyond the reward (e.g. indicating overfitting, as in the example above). Part (b) shows how our method performs design optimization in a loop. Our model Pθ accepts a few-shot context of observations for a design task, including h(x), and predicts the reward f(x) for an unobserved design. These predictions are used to select a promising new design xt+1 for evaluation. The design is evaluated, the new observation is added to the model’s context, and the next iteration begins with this updated context for Pθ. At termination, the design x∗with the highest observed reward is returned. Pθ is trained on a history of design tasks to acquire this few-shot prediction ability (described in Sec. 4).
abstract: Many real-world design problems involve optimizing an expensive black-box function $f(x)$, such as hardware design or drug discovery. Bayesian Optimization has emerged as a sample-efficient framework for this problem. However, the basic setting considered by these methods is simplified compared to real-world experimental setups, where experiments often generate a wealth of useful information. We introduce a new setting where an experiment generates high-dimensional auxiliary information $h(x)$ along with the performance measure $f(x)$; moreover, a history of previously solved tasks from the same task family is available for accelerating optimization. A key challenge of our setting is learning how to represent and utilize $h(x)$ for efficiently solving new optimization tasks beyond the task history. We develop a novel approach for this setting based on a neural model which predicts $f(x)$ for unseen designs given a few-shot context containing observations of $h(x)$. We evaluate our method on two challenging domains, robotic hardware design and neural network hyperparameter tuning, and introduce a novel design problem and large-scale benchmark for the former. On both domains, our method utilizes auxiliary feedback effectively to achieve more accurate few-shot prediction and faster optimization of design tasks, significantly outperforming several methods for multi-task optimization.
